edges.effect_quant: Long-term protection against endometrial cancer is one of the most durable non-contraceptive benefits of combined oral contraceptives. In a 2015 individual-participant meta-analysis of 143,019 women, every 5 years of use was associated with a risk ratio of 0.76 (95% CI 0.73 to 0.78), and older case-control data also showed risk reduction after at least a year of use.
edges.population: women using combined oral contraceptives in the general population
edges.mechanism: Combined oral contraceptives reduce endometrial proliferation by supplying progestogenic opposition to estrogen-driven growth and by suppressing ovulation-related hormonal cycling. That repeated antiproliferative effect gives a biologically plausible explanation for the persistent reduction in endometrial-cancer risk seen years after discontinuation.
edges.summary: The evidence for protection against endometrial cancer is strong and consistent overall. Very large pooled analyses and older case-control studies both indicate that combined oral contraceptive use lowers risk, with greater benefit after longer use and persistence of protection long after the pills are stopped.
edges.caveats: Not every older study was fully consistent, and formulation eras differed substantially. This edge is best read as a robust population-level protective association, not as a guarantee that every formulation or every short course will meaningfully change an individual patient’s absolute risk.

evidence.citation: Collaborative Group on Epidemiological Studies on Endometrial Cancer 2015 Lancet Oncol
evidence.notes: Endometrial cancer and oral contraceptives: an individual participant meta-analysis of 27 276 women with endometrial cancer from 36 epidemiological studies.

effect_quant.comparator: endometrial-cancer risk per 5 years of oral-contraceptive use
